### **Cycle 112 Newsroom Continuity Brief**

This cited continuity brief traces prior events, institutional promises, named citizens, and unresolved storylines across all current **Cycle 112 newsroom leads**, grounded **exclusively** in the published text of *The Cycle Pulse — Y2C110* and *The Cycle Pulse — Y3C7* [1, 2].

---

### **1. West Oakland Stabilization Fund: Month Eleven Clears**

#### **Direct Published Facts**
* **Legislative Origin & Council Vote:** Proposed by **Mayor Avery Santana**, the **West Oakland Stabilization Fund** was signed into law in **Cycle 78** on a **6–3 City Council vote** (recorded votes: **Ramon Vega** yes, **Leonard Tran** no, and **Elliott Crane** yes remotely) with an initial **\$28,000,000 budget** [3-6].
* **Disbursement History & Ledger Milestones:**
  * **Cycle 110 (Month Nine):** Fund Director **Marcus Webb** reported Month-Nine audit data to the Finance Committee: **79 households stabilized in nine months** at a **23-day average processing window** (\$400,000 approved for Month Nine) [1, 3, 4, 7]. The ledger recorded **\$81,188 disbursed in direct household grants** through Cycle 109, carrying **\$23,000,000 remaining** [3, 8].
  * **Cycle 111 / Y3C7 (Month Ten):** Reporter **Carmen Delaine** logged Month-Ten approval of another **\$400,000**, advancing the count to **91 households stabilized** while holding the 23-day processing standard [5, 9-11]. Remaining funds dropped to **\$22,600,000** [5].
  * **City Treasury Context:** The city treasury received \$5,100,000 in Cycle 111 and closed at \$110,300,000 [12].
* **Institutional Positions:**
  * **Mayor Avery Santana:** Announced Month-Ten approval, stating: *"relief without bureaucracy keeps neighbors in their neighborhoods"* [5, 13] and *"the families who qualified for this money six months ago shouldn't wait another day"* [5].
  * **Deputy Mayor Brenda Okoro:** Stated: *"Stabilization is a race against displacement — month-ten disbursement keeps us ahead"* [5, 13].
  * **District 1 Councilmember Denise Carter:** Stated: *"When storefronts go quiet, families go next—so we're taking the Stabilization Fund to where the need is moving"* [6, 8, 14].

#### **Analytical Inferences & Unresolved Storylines for Cycle 112**
* **Accounting Discrepancy:** Editor **Mags Corliss** and Carmen Delaine infer an unresolved arithmetic gap between the initial \$28,000,000 envelope, \$81,188 in early direct grants through C109, and \$22,600,000 remaining [5, 8, 9, 15].
* **Case-Level Processing Times:** A 23-day average hides individual processing delays, and official records do not map specific blocks, tenants, or landlords receiving funds [11, 12, 15, 16].
* **Upcoming Actions:** The **Month-Eleven disbursement review in Cycle 112** and the **Cycle 112 Council vote on the \$4,200,000 West Oakland Tenant Defense Fund** will determine whether public funds accelerate [11, 17].

---

### **2. At 19th Street, the Busiest Station Runs on the Slow Side of the Clock**

#### **Direct Published Facts**
* **Cycle 110 Baseline:** Reporter **Trevor Shimizu** logged 19th St Oakland ridership falling by 999 riders, with on-time performance slipping 7 points to 79% [18].
* **Cycle 111 / Y3C7 Transit Drop:**
  * **19th St Oakland:** Ridership fell sharply by **10,950 riders**, while on-time performance slipped further to **77%** [19].
  * **Systemwide Context:** Total 8-station ridership dropped from 91,564 down to **36,303 boardings** in Cycle 111 during a holiday period with active events [19-21].
  * **Other Stations (Y3C7):** 12th St Oakland City Center dropped 15,192 riders to 8,293 (86% on-time) [22]; West Oakland fell 5,974 riders to 2,706 (84% on-time) [19, 20]; Fruitvale fell 7,557 riders to 4,178 (85% on-time) [19, 20].
* **Field Operator & Transit Staff Observations:**
  * AC Transit bus drivers **Evan Lewis**, **Calvin Mwangi**, and **Ray Neal**, alongside mechanic **Joel Wren**, reported street blockages, dust, and detours around Downtown **Baylight District construction** [19, 23-25].
  * Evan Lewis observed that riders avoid torn-up streets and detours by walking, biking, or staying home, making punctual bus arrivals less useful if platforms remain empty [25].

#### **Analytical Inferences & Unresolved Storylines for Cycle 112**
* **Metrics vs. Use:** Trevor Shimizu and Mags Corliss infer that on-time performance metrics fail to capture rider frustration or platform desertion caused by surface-level construction [23, 25-27].
* **Upcoming Actions:** The upcoming **City Council vote on Baylight District approvals** and route adjustments will test whether transit platform crowds return to 19th Street and 12th Street stations [17, 24, 27].

---

### **3. Aitken's Line Is Earned, Clark's Is Not Yet Tested**

#### **Direct Published Facts**
* **Mark Aitken (First Baseman, Dynasty Veteran):**
  * **World Series Championship:** In Game 5 of the World Series, Aitken homered (1 HR, 1 RBI) alongside Eric Taveras (1 HR, 2 RBI) and Darrin Davis (1 HR, 2 RBI, 3-for-4) to secure the Athletics' seventh championship under General Manager Mike Paulson [28-30].
  * **Parade Bus Reflections:** On the Downtown parade bus, Aitken reflected with Vinnie Keane, Benji Dillon, and Paulson that *"this is it for them... I don't know what's next. None of us do. So yeah, the laugh is easy because we just won a championship — that's real. But the quiet moments on that bus, when everyone's just staring out the window at the crowds? That's where the weight sits. We're not just celebrating a win. We're saying goodbye to something, whether we're ready to or not"* [31-33].
* **Kevin Clark (Third Baseman, Young Hitter):**
  * **2041 Stat Line:** Elliot Marbury’s Data Desk memo audited Clark's 2041 line: 18 games, 64 at-bats, 19 hits, 3 HRs, 3 SOs, 1 BB, .297 AVG, .313 OBP, .547 SLG (1 HR per 21.3 ABs; 1 SO per 21.3 ABs) [34].
  * **Sample Size Limit:** Marbury emphasized that Clark's 64 at-bat sample is far too small to set against veteran Martin Richards's 463 at-bats (who struck out once every 6.6 ABs in 2041) [34-36].
  * **Unconfirmed Speculation:** Feed speculations that Clark's situation mirrors Richards's due to Ernesto Quintero taking everyday DH at-bats carry no official team statement or transaction [34].

#### **Analytical Inferences & Unresolved Storylines for Cycle 112**
* **Line Credibility:** Tanya Cruz, Elliot Marbury, and Mags Corliss infer that while Aitken's career line and championship legacy are fully earned, Clark's statistical profile is unproven [31, 33, 34, 37, 38].
* **Upcoming Actions:** General Manager Mike Paulson's offseason "roster math" regarding free agency, retirements, and whether Aitken, Keane, or Dillon return for 2042 [17, 31, 38].

---

### **4. Uptown's Two Speeds: The Block Moves Faster Than the Store**

#### **Direct Published Facts**
* **Jack London / Port Corridor Revenue Split (Y3C7):**
  * **Port Growth:** Business reporter **Jordan Velez** reported the Port of Oakland’s budget grew by \$765,000 to **\$425,100,000** across 1,501 payroll workers [39]. Harbor tug captain **Elle Lilo**, ship repair foreman **Blair Patel**, container yard supervisor **Dmitri Soto**, and longshoreman **Elena Leon** noted heavy shifts, rising workloads, and glass towers replacing old warehouses [39-42].
  * **Local Dining Ledgers:** Green & Gold Tavern added \$6,000 (to \$3,700,000 across 30 workers including **Hector Leech**, **Trenton Nawan**, **Valentina Campbell**, **Guadalupe Lupe**); Blue Lantern Bar added \$7,000 (to \$3,900,000 across 30 workers including **Yuki Ji**, **Guadalupe Lee**); Harborline Grill added \$1,000 (to \$860,000 across 7 workers including **Tomas Renteria**, **Quynh Le**, **Jalen Hill**, **Bruce Wright**) [43].
  * **Construction Firm:** Anchor Build (managing partner **Marguerite Salcedo**, 181 staff including **Travis Golin**, **Briar Soto**) added \$241,000 to \$146,600,000 [44].
* **Fruitvale Storefront Contrast:** **Jax Caldera** (`JAX-TIPS`) reported Fruitvale taquerias slammed with lunch lines while official city maps log retail vitality dropping 2.04 points and **Housing Pressure climbing +1.00 to 4.5** [45, 46].

#### **Analytical Inferences & Unresolved Storylines for Cycle 112**
* **Lopsided Economy:** Mags Corliss and Jordan Velez infer an uneven economic distribution where corporate capital and real estate development move rapidly while local retail stores and frontline paychecks lag behind [2, 47, 48].
* **Unresolved Storyline:** Whether commercial revenue spillover reaches local storefronts or whether rising rent pressure displaces small merchants [47-50].

---

### **5. Six Names for 142 Sick Residents**

#### **Direct Published Facts**
* **City Illness & Care Baseline:**
  * Official city reports in Cycle 110 identified fog and seasonal respiratory illness events in Lake Merritt and Chinatown [18].
  * In Temescal, **Maria Keen** reported 311 kids, 2,106 working adults, and 294 seniors supported by a single listed care program: the **Temescal Islamic Center Food Pantry** (active since Cycle 83).
  * In Fruitvale, **Jax Caldera** verified that two active roster programs (**Oakland Alternative Response Initiative** and **Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline**) operate in the footprint, but neither owns or mitigates rising housing pressure or health/decay indicators [51, 52].

#### **Analytical Inferences & Unresolved Storylines for Cycle 112**
* **Roster vs. Ownership:** Corliss and Caldera infer that placing a neighborhood inside a program's footprint on paper does not mean any municipal agency is addressing specific resident health and housing needs [9, 51, 52].
* **Unresolved Storyline:** Whether City Hall assigns explicit municipal ownership and healthcare resources to cover concentrated resident illness across Chinatown, Fruitvale, and East Oakland [9, 49, 50, 53].

---

### **6. Culture Scene & Ledger Tracking (`culture_c112_tamsin-pruitt...`)**

#### **Direct Published Facts**
* **Tara Ellison Audit:** In Cycle 111 (Y3C7), **Kai Marston** audited journalist **Tara Ellison**, whom the city culture ledger flagged as "surging/rising" among 39 culture figures in Rockridge [53, 54].
* **Block-Level Disconnect:** On the Rockridge sidewalk, Ellison stated she was *"not in a room with anyone right now"* [54]. Neighboring artists—sculptor **Alma Vasquez** in Laurel and actress **Nina Reyes** in Fruitvale—had not heard of Ellison [55, 56].
* **Fading Figures:** The culture ledger moved names like **Lena Cross** and **Rowan Pierce** to the "where-are-they-now" list [57].

#### **Analytical Inferences & Unresolved Storylines for Cycle 112**
* **Index vs. Street:** Kai Marston and Mags Corliss infer that being counted on a municipal media index is fundamentally disconnected from block-level recognition (*"being counted is one thing; being talked about on the block is another"*) [53, 56, 57].
* **Unresolved Storyline:** Whether newly emerging cultural figures (such as **Tamsin Pruitt** or surging artists) establish authentic street-level presence or remain fleeting statistical entries on municipal dashboards [53, 58].

---

### **Direct Fact vs. Analytical Inference Summary Matrix**

| Current Newsroom Lead | Direct Published Fact (Cycles Y2C110–Y3C7) | Analytical Inference / Unresolved Storyline for Cycle 112 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |

Passed 6–3 in C78 [6]. | Corliss & Delaine infer accounting gap between \$28M budget and \$22.6M remaining [5, 8]. Unresolved: Month-Eleven review & Tenant Defense vote [11, 17]. |

Overall 8-station ridership dropped to 36,303 [21]. | Shimizu & Corliss infer surface construction causes platform desertion [25, 27]. Unresolved: Council vote on Baylight & route fixes [17, 24]. |

Clark logged 18 games / 64 ABs in 2041 [34]. | Cruz & Marbury infer Aitken's line is earned while Clark's sample is too thin [33, 34]. Unresolved: Paulson's roster math on Aitken, Keane, & Dillon [17, 31, 38]. |
| **Uptown's Two Speeds (`Block Moves Faster`)** | Port budget grew by \$765,000 to \$425.1M; local grill revenue added \$1,000 [39, 43]. | Velez & Corliss infer lopsided capital growth favoring industrial firms over local workers [2, 47]. Unresolved: local store survival [48, 49]. |

Fruitvale programs do not own housing pressure [51]. | Corliss & Caldera infer program footprints do not equal active care [9, 52]. Unresolved: assigning municipal ownership to resident illness [49, 50]. |
| **Culture Scene (`tamsin-pruitt...`)** | Tara Ellison flagged as surging in Rockridge, but neighbors Vasquez and Reyes were unaware [54-56]. | Marston infers ledger metrics do not match street-level awareness [53, 58]. Unresolved: whether emerging figures establish genuine block presence [58]. |

references.cited_text: THE CYCLE PULSE — Y2C110 The Bay Tribune — Oakland Narrated by Mags Corliss, Editor-in-Chief ============================================================ Three times this week, someone in Oakland told me something was moving, and three times I went looking for the motion. Start with West Oakland. Marcus Webb told the Finance Committee that seventy-nine households have been stabilized in nine months, and he put it the way a man does when the auditors are in the room: families with checks in hand before the notices arrive, every dollar moving through compliance. Carmen Delaine reported the fund's pace, a little over three weeks from application to money. Mayor Santana called it "relief without bureaucracy." Those two ideas sit uncomfortably together. A fund that is proud of how well it passes scrutiny is not a fund without bureaucracy. It may be a good bureaucracy, and I'd rather have a careful one than a reckless one, but let's not pretend it's something else.

THE CYCLE PULSE — Y3C7 The Bay Tribune — Oakland Narrated by Mags Corliss, Editor-in-Chief ============================================================ The week came down to a gap between what gets counted and what gets felt, and I kept finding that gap in every desk's copy. Start at the water. Jordan Velez reported that the Port's books grew, and then he went and asked the people doing the work. Elle Lilo, who captains a harbor tug, told him her day hasn't changed much and the bustle is just louder. Blair Patel, a ship repair foreman, called the growth a double-edged sword with a relentless pace. Dmitri Soto, who runs the container yard, said the job is bigger than stacking boxes now. My father worked the docks for thirty years, and I know what "busier" usually means. The shift gets heavier first, and the paycheck is a separate conversation. Jordan carried the question inland to the dining rooms and bar rails, where a port's growth is supposed to land. Guadalupe Lupe, Hector Leech and Trenton Nawan turn up in his business reporting and again in Mason Ortega's culture pages. Briar Soto turns up in Jordan's work too. I'll say what I can say honestly: the same people are being read as commerce in one section and as culture in another. Nobody in this city lives in a single desk. A bar rail is a balance sheet and a scene at once, and when the money lands unevenly, the scene feels it.

The West Oakland Stabilization Fund, proposed by Mayor Avery Santana and signed into law in Cycle 78 with a 6-3 council vote, is now moving checks through the real machinery of bureaucracy. Cycle 110 marked the ninth month of active disbursement, and the Initiative_Tracker logs the arc: $400,000 approved for Month-Nine, with a 23-day average processing window achieved. The fund's total envelope was $28 million. It has disbursed, in visible tranche, $81,188 in household grants by the end of Cycle 109, and now carries $23 million remaining.

What the tracker shows: a 23-day average processing window in Month Nine. What it does not show, and what no official present offered: how many applications were received, how many were denied, what the demographic footprint of the seventy-nine households looks like, or whether the fund is keeping pace with displacement pressure in the neighborhood or falling behind it. The Finance Committee scrutiny that Webb cited is real—it appears in the Initiative_Tracker as a control gate. The vote itself, in Cycle 78, was narrow: 6-3, with Ramon Vega voting yes, Leonard Tran voting no, and Elliott Crane voting yes remotely. The remaining seats were not named in the record supplied. The fund was designed for West Oakland, the economic policy domain was explicit, and the disbursement phase is active now.

The money is real and it is moving. The West Oakland Stabilization Fund carries a $28,000,000 budget, with $22,600,000 still remaining, and its latest disbursement landed this cycle, Cycle 111: a month-ten payment of $400,000. Avery Santana, who proposed the Fund, announced that approval in two statements. "Month-ten disbursement approved — $400,000 to keep West Oakland families in their homes," she said at the gavel. At the open, she added: "The families who qualified for this money six months ago shouldn't wait another day." Brenda Okoro put the stakes in the same terms: "Stabilization is a race against displacement — month-ten disbursement keeps us ahead."

The Fund's path to this point runs through a single vote. In Cycle 78 the measure passed 6-3, against a required threshold of 6-3, and Santana signed it that cycle. The record names three of the nine seats: Ramon Vega voted yes, Leonard Tran voted no, and Elliott Crane voted yes remotely. The file does not place the other six, and this ledger will not infer them from a tally. Denise Carter, whose District 1 office issued this cycle's council statement, framed the Fund's reach around movement rather than fixed addresses: "When storefronts go quiet, families go next—so we're taking the Stabilization Fund to where the need is moving." That sentence points at a geography the tracker does not map. The Initiative is logged to West Oakland, and nothing in the file breaks the $400,000 down by block, by household, or by case.

============================================================ THE WEEK'S REPORTING By Carmen Delaine | Bay Tribune Civic Nine Months, Seventy-Nine Households: The Stabilization Fund Moves at a 23-Day Pace By Carmen Delaine Marcus Webb sat in the Finance Committee chamber with a single line of data that carried the weight of displacement pressure: seventy-nine households stabilized in nine months. He framed the number not as a victory lap but as evidence of traction. "Seventy-nine households stabilized means seventy-nine Oakland families with checks in hand before the displacement notices arrive," Webb said, his tone calibrated to the auditors tracking compliance. Every dollar, he added, moves with the compliance that passes the Finance Committee's scrutiny.

There is also a gap in the arithmetic nobody has explained. The fund was sized at $28 million. Carmen's reporting has about $81,000 in household grants out the door by the end of last cycle, and the same reporting puts the remainder at $23 million. Those figures don't reconcile. Maybe the difference is money committed but not yet paid, or money in another category. Maybe it's a reporting slip. Webb and the Finance Committee can tell us which. Denise Carter said it plainly, "When storefronts go quiet, families go next," and if that's the thesis, residents deserve a clear answer on how much of the money is actually reaching them.

Jax Caldera found the mirror image in Fruitvale, a lunch line out the door at the taqueria while the neighborhood's own readings slide. Mood is still near the top of the city and retail still sits well above the middle, but both are dropping and housing pressure is climbing. Two programs list Fruitvale in their footprint, and neither owns the problem that's actually hurting it. Jax asked who answers for that, and no one with a title would say. I'd add one thing. Carmen Delaine reported on the West Oakland Stabilization Fund, where Marcus Webb says ninety-one households are stabilized and every file will survive an audit. Another $400,000 went out this week, and the processing standard held at twenty-three days. Carmen was honest that an average hides the slowest case, and the record doesn't show whether any family waited far longer. Councilmember Denise Carter said the Fund is being taken to where the need is moving. Fine. Jax is standing in a place where the need appears to be moving, and the Fund isn't listed there.

============================================================ By Carmen Delaine | Bay Tribune Civic Ninety-One Households, One Ledger "Ninety-one households stabilized means ninety-one West Oakland families who won't face displacement this month," Marcus Webb said on the record this cycle, "and every case file meets compliance standards that will survive audit." The statement is the only place in this cycle's record where the Stabilization Fund is counted by household rather than by dollar, and it is the figure the city is standing on.

The clock is the strongest part of the record. Month-nine, in Cycle 110, cleared at $400,000 with a 23-day average processing time. Cycle 111 held the 23-day processing standard again. The next action is the month-eleven disbursement review in Cycle 112. An average is a single number, and the file carries no case-level processing times. A 23-day mean can hold cases that took far longer, and the record does not say whether any did. Two neighboring Initiatives show the same pattern of announced money and thin public accounting. The West Oakland Tenant Defense Fund is scheduled for a vote in Cycle 112 at a $4.2M budget. Commercial Stabilization for Grand Lake sits at legislation-filed with $2.5M. Neither is in disbursement, and neither has a payment on the books this cycle.

What the Packet does establish is this: the Fund moved $400,000 on schedule, the processing standard held, and the city's account of the families involved is one household count and one compliance claim, both from the office that runs the Fund. What it does not establish is where the money lands once it leaves the treasury, which block, which tenant, or which landlord. The city treasury took in $5.1M this cycle and closed at $110.3M, and nothing in the file traces the Fund's dollars through that balance.

Mayor Santana pressed the speed narrative. "Nine months in, we're proving that relief without bureaucracy keeps neighbors in their neighborhoods," she said in her cycle-110 office record. The claim nested two things: that the mechanism was working, and that other cities or prior efforts had let bureaucracy be the obstacle. Brenda Okoro, in her own statement, refined it further. "Nine months in, the Fund's design is holding—targeted relief that flows to tenants before displacement does," she said. The sequence matters—relief first, displacement second, not the other way around.

The name of the game, as framed by the officials steering it, is speed wrapped in compliance. That friction—moving cash without creating audit liability—is where the story sits this cycle. Denise Carter, City Council District 1, had already staked her position earlier in the cycle on where that friction resolves. "When storefronts go quiet, families go next—so we're taking the Stabilization Fund to where the need is moving," she said. The language was deliberate: the fund is not a static account waiting for applications; it is a tool meant to track and intercept displacement as it moves. The implication was that West Oakland's commercial core and its residential stability are yoked.

Webb's ninety-one families are a real number in a real statement. They are not yet a place on a map or a name in a file the public can read. Ask who should answer the question the disbursement invites. The Stabilization Fund's office signed the audit claim. The mayor's office announced the payment. The council seat that moved the Fund toward "where the need is moving" has not said where that is in the record this cycle. If the money is moving on time, why can't the city show us where it lands? INTAKE

The next scheduled action is Month-Ten disbursement review in Cycle 111. That checkpoint will show whether the 23-day window holds, whether the pace of cash flow accelerates or stalls, and whether the remaining $23 million carries the same gravity in the tenth month as it did in the ninth. The extraction question Webb's own language raised but could not answer: Are seventy-nine households enough to hold the line in West Oakland's commercial districts before the next wave of displacement notices arrive?

Next week I'm watching the month-eleven review for the Stabilization Fund, and whether the case-level times ever come out. I'm watching the council vote on Baylight and whether the platform fills back in. I'm watching Paulson's roster math, and Aitken's name in particular. I'm watching whether anyone claims Fruitvale. And I'm watching the Oaks as their season opens, to see whether anyone in that bar glances back at the screen. ============================================================ THE WEEK'S REPORTING

Lake Merritt moved down more than any other station in the cycle’s eight-station comparison. The change did not arrive with a single reported closure or interruption. The available record identifies fog and events in Lake Merritt and Chinatown, but it does not establish which of those conditions mattered most. The station’s numbers show the result, not the cause. The broader pattern is uneven. MacArthur lost 2,034 riders and fell six points in on-time performance, to 78 percent. Coliseum lost 1,701 riders and fell seven points, to 76 percent. Rockridge lost 1,699 riders and fell three points, to 75 percent. At 19th St Oakland, ridership fell 999 and on-time performance fell seven points, to 79 percent. At 12th St Oakland City Center, the decline was smaller—363 riders—with on-time performance down four points, to 81 percent.

The same separation appears elsewhere. Nineteen St Oakland fell by 10,950 riders while its on-time result slipped to 77%. West Oakland fell by 5,974 while on-time performance rose nine points, to 84%. Fruitvale fell by 7,557 while on-time performance rose seven points, to 85%. The pattern is not limited to one station or one kind of schedule. Ray Neal, an AC Transit Bus Operator, described the operational symptom without assigning it a cause. “You know, it’s quieter now. Fewer folks waiting, fewer folks boarding. Feels like the energy’s shifted somewhere else, but I can’t quite put my finger on where.”

But Fruitvale moved in the other direction. It gained 1,321 riders, reaching 11,735, even as on-time performance fell three points to 78 percent. West Oakland gained 45 riders, to 8,680, while its on-time performance fell six points to 75 percent. That split is the important infrastructure fact. The system did not simply become less used everywhere. Across the eight stations and ten corridors measured, total ridership fell to 91,564 from 99,582. The station-level changes point to a network that is carrying different kinds of pressure in different places. Lake Merritt’s decline is the sharpest, but Fruitvale’s increase prevents a clean explanation based only on fog or general movement.

Across the eight stations, ridership totaled 36,303 in Cycle 111, compared with 91,564 in the prior cycle. That is a large change in the system’s use, but the record also marks the cycle as a holiday period with events in Downtown, Fruitvale, Dimond, East Oakland, Jack London, Rockridge and Piedmont Ave. Those conditions complicate any clean explanation. A quieter platform can be the result of construction, a holiday pattern, changed destinations, or several pressures operating together. Evan Lewis, a bus driver, put the gap between the dashboard and the sidewalk more directly.

============================================================ By Trevor Shimizu | Bay Tribune Civic 12th Street Is Running Better. The People Are Somewhere Else. By Trevor Shimizu At 7:40 at 12th St Oakland City Center, Joel Wren was looking at a quieter station and a smoother service. The station recorded 8,293 riders in Cycle 111, down 15,192 from the previous cycle. Its on-time performance improved to 86%, five points higher than before. Those two measurements are supposed to describe the same transit system. Here they do not.

“I’ve been noticing fewer folks at the 12th Street station lately, even though the buses are running smoother than ever,” Wren said. “It’s strange—people used to pack in there, but now it feels quieter. Maybe it’s the Baylight construction approvals making folks rethink their routes. Hard to say, but something’s shifted.” The fare gate continues its small mechanical argument with each person who uses it. The schedule can be better while the station becomes less useful. On-time performance measures whether service arrives when expected. Ridership measures whether people still choose to be there. A system can improve the first measure and lose the second.

Calvin Mwangi, an AC Transit bus driver, said he has not heard regular riders identify 12th Street as a specific avoidance point. “Nah, can't say I've heard my regulars talk much about avoiding 12th Street specifically,” Mwangi said. “Most folks just grumble about the usual—delays, construction, you know how it is. But no, nothing about the council vote coming up in conversation.” That distinction matters. The record does not establish that Baylight District construction caused the missing riders. It does establish that Baylight District construction is active around Downtown, while the station posted its largest decline among the eight stations tracked this cycle. Construction is a plausible explanation, not a completed diagnosis.

“You know, it's funny—on paper, the numbers look good, right? Better on-time stats should mean happier riders. But driving the route, I see it different. When they start tearing up streets for these big projects, people just... find another way. Doesn't matter if the bus shows up on time if the sidewalks are blocked and the air's full of dust. Folks in my neighborhood talk about it at the stop—they're tired of detours and noise, so they walk, bike, or just stay home. The stats don't show that frustration.”

The same split shows up in transit. Trevor Shimizu reported that the 12th Street station ran better and emptied out at the same time. Service got more punctual while a huge number of riders simply weren't there. Joel Wren said it plainly: people used to pack in, and now it's quiet. Trevor was careful, and I'll be too. Baylight construction is a plausible reason, not a proven one. Calvin Mwangi, who drives the bus, hasn't heard his regulars say they're dodging the station. Other stations showed the same pattern, with trains on time and platforms thin. A system can improve the thing it measures and lose the thing it's for.

The infrastructure question is therefore not only whether a bus arrives on time. It is whether the full path to the bus remains attractive enough to use. Cycle 111 shows a service that is, in several places, more punctual and less occupied. That balance is the real Jack London story this cycle. It does not show up in the Port's top line. It shows up in how unevenly the money lands once it leaves the water. Start at the repair end.
